analysis.one_liner: Requires newly formed corporations and LLCs to disclose their real human owners to federal law enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a Democrat with one Republican cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone forming a corporation or limited liability company in a state that does not already collect it to file the names, addresses, and identification numbers of the company's real owners ("beneficial owners") with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. It would impose civil penalties up to $10,000 and up to three years in prison for filing false ownership information or willfully failing to file, require companies that sell incorporation services to run anti-money-laundering programs, and give federal contractors' ownership information to procurement officials. The stated purpose is to stop criminals from hiding behind anonymous American shell companies to launder money, evade taxes, finance terrorism, and commit fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit indirectly but materially: the bill gives law enforcement a way to see who actually owns a company, which is the tool investigators say they lack when tracing fraud, money laundering, drug trafficking, and terrorism financing run through American shell companies. It also helps honest small businesses and banks, who are often defrauded by counterparties whose true owners cannot be identified.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fraud victims, law enforcement, honest small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Requires corporations and LLCs formed in states without disclosure rules to file their beneficial owners' names, addresses, and passport or driver's license numbers with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, with updates within 60 days of any change.

Imposes a civil penalty of up to $10,000 and criminal penalties of up to three years in prison for knowingly filing false or fraudulent beneficial ownership information or willfully failing to provide complete or updated information.

Requires people in the business of forming companies (formation agents) to establish anti-money-laundering programs under the Bank Secrecy Act framework, closing the gap where incorporation services faced no such obligations.

Makes beneficial ownership information available to federal and state investigators by subpoena, to Congress, to foreign countries through treaty channels, and to banks doing required customer due diligence with the customer's consent.

Requires federal contractors above a small-purchase threshold to disclose their beneficial owners as part of bids, helping procurement officials screen out companies owned by sanctioned or fraudulent actors.

Exempts large companies (more than 20 full-time US employees, over $5 million in gross receipts, and a US office), regulated banks, insurers, investment companies, and registered nonprofits, concentrating the burden on small and new entities.

analysis.who_pays: The people forming small and new companies bear a new reporting burden — providing identification for each real owner and keeping it current, with penalties for willful failures. Formation agents and state filing offices must build systems to collect and safeguard the data, though the bill authorizes up to $30 million from the Treasury forfeiture fund and $10 million from the Justice forfeiture fund to reimburse state compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Small business founders and incorporation service companies

drawbacks.text: Founders of small companies and LLCs — the entities still covered after the large-company exemptions — would face recurring paperwork: owner identification at formation, updates within 60 days of any ownership change, and annual filings.

The bill channels sensitive personal identifying information (home addresses, passport and license numbers) into state and federal databases, creating data-breach risk, while it explicitly leaves verification of the submitted information to the states' discretion and bars Treasury from requiring the data be filed with the IRS.
Attorneys and law firms that use a paid formation agent are excluded from the new anti-money-laundering obligations, a carve-out critics could point to as a gap in coverage.

The bill takes a federalist approach: states that adopt compliant systems keep their incorporation business, and the Treasury Secretary cannot withhold other federal funding from a state that fails to comply, relying on a GAO compliance report instead of enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but modest: paperwork for small-entity founders, which the exemptions deliberately limit to smaller players, plus a funded build-out for states. The benefit is a structural fix to a problem investigators, the Financial Action Task Force, and the bill's own findings document at length — the ease of forming an anonymous US company in under an hour — with penalties aimed at people who lie about ownership. On balance a reasonable trade, though the no-verification and no-funding-withholding provisions weaken its teeth.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on August 2, 2017, read twice, and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up or reported it out before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on August 2, 2017, joined by Sen. Marco Rubio as its sole cosponsor, making it a bipartisan introduction from the start.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action of any kind appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress.
No committee markup, no floor vote, and no House companion action is recorded; the bill died at the committee stage when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: people and businesses that profit from forming anonymous US companies — formation agents and the states that market quick, owner-free incorporation — kept operating as before, and wrongdoers relying on shell-company anonymity kept the gap the bill described.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in sponsorship — one Democrat and one Republican — but it never advanced far enough for a vote, so no roll-call shows where the broader parties stood.

industries.industry: Company formation agents and registered agent services
industries.note: The bill would put incorporation service companies under Bank Secrecy Act anti-money-laundering obligations and attach civil and criminal penalties to failing to keep verified owner information. Their core product — fast, anonymous company formation — is what the bill targets, and the bill's own findings note websites advertising that anonymity alongside offshore jurisdictions.

industries.industry: State incorporation franchises (state filing offices and the businesses around them)
industries.note: States would have to collect and retain beneficial ownership data (or lose formation traffic to federal filing), but the bill preserves their role, funds compliance up to $40 million from forfeiture funds, and even lets states restrict public access to the data. For states whose filing fees and franchise rest on quick, anonymous formation, this is a real cost; the state interest in keeping that product has run against the law-enforcement purpose.

Banks get a route to beneficial ownership information (with customer consent) for the customer due diligence they are already required to perform, reducing fraud and compliance risk they currently absorb.

industries.industry: Small business owners forming new entities
industries.note: Small-entity founders face new reporting duties and penalty exposure; large companies, banks, insurers, and registered nonprofits are exempted, so the burden lands on the smallest players. Honest small businesses also stand to gain from a marketplace with fewer shell-company fraudsters.
